questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR → Part 152 → § 152.103 (Transaction value: PAPP, Statutory Additions & Exclusions)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Start with the CIF invoice total ($115,000) and determine which international shipment charges must be deducted to arrive at the base Price Actually Paid or Payable (PAPP).

Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 152 → § 152.103(b)(1) to check the five statutory additions to PAPP, and cross-reference § 152.102(a) to see which buyer-supplied items qualify as dutiable assists.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Buying commissions ($4,000) and U.S.-undertaken engineering/design sketches ($6,000) are NEVER added! Add only the mold assist including its freight to the foreign factory ($8,000 + $500) and the condition-of-sale patent royalty ($3,500).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 152.103(a)(1) and (i)(1), international ocean freight ($11,000) and marine cargo insurance ($1,500) are excluded from the CIF price ($115,000) because they are separately itemized, yielding a base Price Actually Paid or Payable (PAPP) of $102,500 ($115,000 - $12,500). Next, under § 152.103(b)(1), we add: (1) the mold assist value of $8,500 ($8,000 acquisition cost + $500 freight to transport the mold to the foreign factory per § 152.102(a)(3)); and (2) the $3,500 patent royalty because the buyer is required to pay it as a condition of the sale for exportation to the U.S. under § 152.103(b)(1)(iv). The $4,000 buying commission is excluded (only selling commissions are added under § 152.103(b)(1)(ii)), and the $6,000 design work undertaken in the United States is excluded from the definition of an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) & (a)(2). Calculation: $102,500 + $8,500 + $3,500 = $114,500.

distractors.A: $102,500 is the net FOB Price Actually Paid or Payable ($115,000 - $11,000 freight - $1,500 insurance), but it omits the mandatory statutory additions for the mold assist ($8,500) and the condition-of-sale royalty ($3,500).
distractors.B: CORRECT ($114,500): Net PAPP of $102,500 + $8,500 mold assist (including transport to the factory) + $3,500 condition-of-sale royalty.
distractors.C: $118,500 erroneously includes the $4,000 bona fide buying commission. Under 19 CFR § 152.103(b)(1)(ii), only selling commissions incurred by the buyer are added to PAPP.
distractors.D: $120,500 erroneously includes the $6,000 design sketches created in Seattle. Under 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1)(iv), engineering and design work is an assist only when undertaken OUTSIDE the United States.
distractors.E: $127,000 fails to deduct the separately itemized $11,000 international ocean freight and $1,500 marine cargo insurance from the CIF invoice price ($114,500 + $12,500).

questions.stem: Pacific Rim Forwarding LLC, an unlicensed ocean freight forwarder, refers a new U.S. importer, Cascade Home Furnishings Inc., to licensed customs broker Maria Vance. Pacific Rim asks Vance to pay a referral commission of $35 per customs entry filed on behalf of Cascade Home Furnishings and requests that Vance send her brokerage invoices to Pacific Rim so that Pacific Rim can bundle all logistics and customs charges onto a single consolidated invoice to Cascade. Under 19 CFR § 111.36, under what exact conditions may Broker Vance legally compensate Pacific Rim Forwarding for the referral?

options.text: A licensed customs broker is strictly prohibited under all circumstances from sharing fees or paying referral compensation to an unlicensed person or freight forwarder.

Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided she obtains prior written approval from the Center of Excellence and Expertise (CEE) Director and caps the referral fee at 10% of the brokerage charge.
Vance may compensate the freight forwarder only if Cascade purchases the goods on a Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) basis and the forwarder acts as the Importer of Record.

Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided she notifies the importer in advance in writing of the name of the forwarder being compensated, transmits a true copy of her brokerage charges directly to the importer (unless waived in writing by the importer), and the forwarder neither controls the brokerage fees nor forbids direct communication between the broker and the importer.
Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided the forwarder rebates at least 50% of the referral commission back to the importer as a volume discount.

questions.goldenQuote: (1) The importer is notified in advance in writing by the broker of the name of the freight forwarder who is being compensated by the broker for the referral;
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Look for the specific regulatory exception to the general rule against fee-splitting with unlicensed persons when the unlicensed party is a freight forwarder.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Navigate to 19 CFR Part 111 → § 111.36 and read paragraph (c) ('Compensation of freight forwarder').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check all 5 cumulative conditions in § 111.36(c)(1)-(5): advance written notice to the importer, direct transmittal of the brokerage bill (unless waived in writing), no control of fees by the forwarder, no ban on direct communication, and NO sharing of the referral fee with the importer.

explanation.correctReasoning: While 19 CFR § 111.36(b) generally prohibits a broker from entering into fee-splitting agreements where brokerage benefits inure to an unlicensed person, § 111.36(c) carves out an explicit exception allowing a broker to compensate a freight forwarder for referring brokerage business if five strict conditions are met: (1) advance written notice to the importer identifying the forwarder being compensated; (2) direct transmission to the importer of a true copy of the brokerage charges when collected through the forwarder (unless waived in writing by the importer); (3) the forwarder does not control or prescribe brokerage fees or conditions; (4) the forwarder does not forbid direct communication between importer and broker; and (5) no part of the compensation is shared with or refunded to the importer.

distractors.A: Incorrect because 19 CFR § 111.36(c) expressly authorizes compensating a freight forwarder for referrals when the five conditions in paragraph (c) are satisfied.
distractors.B: Incorrect because CBP regulations do not require CEE Director approval or impose a 10% percentage cap on freight forwarder referral fees.
distractors.C: Incorrect because DDP terms apply to the exception in § 111.36(a) regarding employment by an unlicensed intermediary, not the referral compensation requirements in § 111.36(c).
distractors.D: CORRECT: Accurately states the cumulative requirements of 19 CFR § 111.36(c)(1)–(4).
distractors.E: Incorrect because 19 CFR § 111.36(c)(5) explicitly prohibits sharing or refunding any part of the forwarder's referral compensation to the importer or any officer/employee of the importer.

questions.stem:
Meridian Retail Group imports two different packaged products in shrink-wrapped retail display boxes ready for direct sale to consumers without repacking:
• Product 1 ('Executive Commuter Gift Box'): Contains one ceramic insulated travel coffee mug (Heading 6912, value $8.00), one pair of knitted merino wool dress socks (Heading 6115, value $9.00), and one stainless-steel ballpoint pen (Heading 9608, value $7.50).
• Product 2 ('At-Home Pasta Dinner Kit'): Contains one box of uncooked dry durum wheat spaghetti (Heading 1902, value $3.20), one sealed pouch of tomato basil pasta sauce (Heading 2103, value $1.80), and one small packet of grated Parmesan cheese (Heading 0406, value $0.90).

Under the General Rules of Interpretation (GRI), how must Product 1 and Product 2 be classified?

options.text: Both Product 1 and Product 2 qualify as retail sets under GRI 3(b); Product 1 is classified entirely in Heading 6115 (highest value component), and Product 2 is classified entirely in Heading 1902.

Both Product 1 and Product 2 qualify as retail sets under GRI 3(b), but because no single component imparts essential character to Product 1, Product 1 is classified in Heading 9608 under GRI 3(c) (last in numerical order), while Product 2 is classified in Heading 1902.

Product 1 FAILS the GRI 3(b) retail set test because its articles are not put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity, so the mug (6912), socks (6115), and pen (9608) must each be classified separately; Product 2 QUALIFIES as a GRI 3(b) retail set and is classified as a single unit under Heading 1902 (the pasta component imparting essential character).
Neither Product 1 nor Product 2 qualifies as a retail set under GRI 3(b) because food items and consumer gift items must always be classified separately under GRI 1.
Product 1 is classified as a retail set under GRI 3(c) in Heading 9608, whereas each food item in Product 2 must be classified separately under Headings 1902, 2103, and 0406.

questions.targetCitation: HTSUS GRI 3(b) & Explanatory Note X (3-Prong Retail Set Test)
questions.goldenQuote: (2) Consist of products or articles put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity (Note: If a retail package contains disparate items that do NOT work together toward a single specific activity—for example, a promotional gift basket containing a ceramic coffee mug, a pair of cotton socks, and a ballpoint pen—it FAILS prong 2, is NOT a GRI 3(b) set, and EVERY item must be classified separately under its own HTSUS heading!); and
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI → GRI 1–6 → HTSUS GRI 3 (Rule 3(b) Retail Sets 3-Prong Test)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Before applying 'essential character' under GRI 3(b) or 'last in numerical order' under GRI 3(c), verify whether each retail package legally qualifies as 'goods put up in sets for retail sale'.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI → GRI 1–6 → HTSUS GRI 3 and examine the Mandatory 3-Prong Test for retail sets under GRI 3(b).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check Prong 2 ('put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity'). Do a coffee mug, socks, and a pen work together to perform a single activity? No! Therefore Product 1 fails Prong 2 and each item classifies separately, whereas Product 2 (spaghetti, sauce, Parmesan) combines to prepare a pasta meal.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 3(b) and Explanatory Note X, a package qualifies as 'goods put up in sets for retail sale' ONLY if it satisfies all three prongs: (1) at least two articles prima facie classifiable in different headings; (2) put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity; and (3) packaged for direct retail sale without repacking. Product 1 (a ceramic mug, wool socks, and a ballpoint pen) consists of disparate items that do not interact to carry out a specific activity (drinking coffee, dressing one's feet, and writing are unrelated activities). Because Product 1 fails Prong 2, it is NOT a GRI 3(b) set, and each item must be classified separately under GRI 1 (Headings 6912, 6115, and 9608). Conversely, Product 2 (spaghetti, pasta sauce, and grated Parmesan) satisfies all three prongs because the ingredients are used together to prepare a spaghetti meal, and the spaghetti (Heading 1902) imparts the essential character of the set under GRI 3(b).

distractors.A: Incorrect because Product 1 fails Prong 2 of the GRI 3(b) retail set definition; disparate gift items cannot be grouped under the highest-value item.
distractors.B: Incorrect because GRI 3(c) ('last in numerical order') applies to sets only AFTER a package first qualifies as a valid retail set under GRI 3(b). Since Product 1 fails the retail set test, GRI 3(c) cannot be invoked.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Product 1 fails Prong 2 (no unified specific activity) and is classified item-by-item, while Product 2 satisfies all three prongs of GRI 3(b) and is classified by its essential character (Heading 1902).
distractors.D: Incorrect because multi-ingredient meal kits whose components are prepared together into a single dish (like a pasta dinner kit) are classic examples of valid GRI 3(b) retail sets.
distractors.E: Incorrect because it reverses the legal outcome for both products.

questions.stem: A container vessel carrying non-quota commercial machinery arrives within the port limits of Savannah, GA and lands its cargo on Monday, November 2. On Tuesday, November 3, the licensed customs broker transmits the entry documentation (CBP Form 3461 electronic equivalent) without an entry summary and without requesting an immediate time-of-entry election upon filing. On Wednesday, November 4, CBP authorizes the release of the merchandise. Wednesday, November 11 is Veterans Day (a federal holiday). Under 19 CFR § 141.68 and § 142.12, what is the 'time of entry' for this shipment, and what is the final deadline for the broker to file the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached without incurring liquidated damages?

options.text: Time of entry is Monday, November 2; the Entry Summary is due no later than Tuesday, November 17 (15 calendar days after landing).
Time of entry is Tuesday, November 3; the Entry Summary is due no later than Tuesday, November 17 (10 working days after filing CBP Form 3461).
Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4; the Entry Summary is due no later than Wednesday, November 18 (10 working days after time of entry, Including Veterans Day).

Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4; the Entry Summary is due no later than Thursday, November 19 (10 working days after time of entry, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and the Veterans Day federal holiday).
Time of entry is Thursday, November 19 (when the Entry Summary is filed); the Entry Summary is due within 30 calendar days after release.

questions.goldenQuote: When the entry documentation is filed before the entry summary, the importer or broker must file the entry summary (CBP Form 7501 or ACE electronic equivalent), with estimated duties attached (or scheduled via Automated Clearinghouse / Periodic Monthly Statement), within 10 working days after the time of entry (as determined under § 141.68).
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR → Part 142 → § 142.12 (Time for filing entry summary)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): First determine the 'time of entry' under 19 CFR § 141.68(a)(1) when CBP Form 3461 is filed without an entry summary and without a special filing-time request.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 142 → § 142.12(b) and (c) to see the exact deadline for filing Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) after the time of entry.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Count 10 WORKING days starting on the day AFTER CBP authorizes release (Release = Wed, Nov 4 -> Day 1 = Thu, Nov 5). Exclude Sat/Sun (Nov 7–8), Wed Nov 11 (Veterans Day federal holiday), and Sat/Sun (Nov 14–15).

explanation.correctReasoning: First, under 19 CFR § 141.68(a)(1), when entry documentation (CBP Form 3461) is filed without an entry summary and the importer has not requested time of entry at filing, the 'time of entry' is the time CBP authorizes the release of the merchandise—here, Wednesday, November 4. Second, under 19 CFR § 142.12(b) and (c), the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached must be filed within 10 working days after the time of entry, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays. Counting working days starting the day after November 4: Day 1 = Thu Nov 5; Day 2 = Fri Nov 6; [Sat Nov 7 & Sun Nov 8 excluded]; Day 3 = Mon Nov 9; Day 4 = Tue Nov 10; [Wed Nov 11 excluded for Veterans Day federal holiday]; Day 5 = Thu Nov 12; Day 6 = Fri Nov 13; [Sat Nov 14 & Sun Nov 15 excluded]; Day 7 = Mon Nov 16; Day 8 = Tue Nov 17; Day 9 = Wed Nov 18; Day 10 = Thursday, November 19.

distractors.A: Confuses the 10-working-day Entry Summary deadline (§ 142.12(b)) with the 15-calendar-day initial entry filing window after landing before merchandise goes to General Order (§ 142.2(a)).
distractors.B: Erroneously uses the date CBP Form 3461 was submitted (Nov 3) as the time of entry without an importer election under § 141.68(a)(2) and fails to exclude Veterans Day.
distractors.C: Correctly identifies Wednesday, November 4 as the time of entry, but fails to exclude Wednesday, November 11 (Veterans Day federal holiday) when counting 10 working days.
distractors.D: CORRECT: Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4 (release authorization), and Day 10 of working days (excluding weekends and Veterans Day) is Thursday, November 19.
distractors.E: Confuses standard consumption entry release (§ 141.68(a)) with Immediate Delivery release (§ 141.68(c)), where time of entry is when the entry summary is filed, and states a non-existent 30-day deadline.

questions.stem: On March 10, 2024, Precision Optics Corp. imported 1,000 laser rangefinders classified under HTSUS subheading 9015.10.4000 ('Rangefinders: Electrical', duty rate 5% ad valorem; note that the 8-digit subheading 9015.10.40 description does NOT begin with the word 'Other'). The entered value was $200.00 per unit ($200,000 total), and Precision Optics paid $10,000.00 in customs duties ($10.00 duty per unit). On August 15, 2026, Precision Optics exported 1,000 unused domestic rangefinders to Germany that were never used in the United States and are also classified under HTSUS 9015.10.4000, but have a lower commercial export invoice value of $150.00 per unit ($150,000 total). Precision Optics timely files a TFTEA Unused Merchandise Substitution Drawback claim (19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2)) in ACE designating the 1,000 imported units (ignoring MPF for this calculation). Under 19 CFR § 190.32, what is the maximum drawback duty refund allowable on this claim?

options.text: $0.00, because the exported rangefinders were domestically produced and have a different unit value than the imported rangefinders.

questions.goldenQuote: (c) Amount of drawback — The "Lesser Of" Rule. For unused merchandise substitution drawback claims under 19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2), the total amount of drawback allowable will not exceed 99 percent of the LESSER of:
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR → Part 190 → § 190.32 (Unused merchandise substitution drawback & 'lesser of' rule)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under TFTEA Modernized Drawback, unused substitution (19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2)) is based on matching 8-digit HTSUS classification, but the refund amount is subject to a statutory value comparison cap.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 190 → § 190.32 and read paragraph (c) ('Amount of drawback — The "Lesser Of" Rule').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Compare the duty paid on the imported units ($200,000 × 5% = $10,000) against the duty that would apply to the lower-valued substituted exported units ($150,000 × 5% = $7,500). Take the LESSER amount ($7,500) and multiply by the 99% drawback rate ($7,500 × 0.99)!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 190.32(a) and (b)(1), unused merchandise substitution drawback under 19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2) is valid because both the designated imported merchandise and the substituted exported domestic merchandise are classified under the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading (9015.10.40, which does not begin with 'Other') and exportation occurred within 5 years of importation. However, under § 190.32(c) (the TFTEA 'Lesser Of' Rule), the drawback refund is capped at 99% of the LESSER of: (1) the duties paid on the designated imported merchandise ($200/unit × 1,000 units × 5% = $10,000.00), OR (2) the duties that would have applied to the substituted exported merchandise had it been imported at that rate ($150/unit × 1,000 units × 5% = $7,500.00). Since $7,500.00 is less than $10,000.00, we apply the 99% refund limit to $7,500.00: $7,500.00 × 0.99 = $7,425.00.

distractors.A: Incorrect because 19 CFR § 190.32(a) explicitly permits substituting domestic or imported merchandise classified under the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading regardless of price differences.
distractors.B: CORRECT ($7,425.00): 99% of the lesser duty amount ($150,000 substituted export value × 5% duty rate = $7,500.00 × 99% = $7,425.00).
distractors.C: $7,500.00 applies the 'lesser of' cap correctly ($150,000 × 5%) but forgets to reduce the refund by the mandatory 1% CBP retention (99% drawback limit).
distractors.D: $9,900.00 is 99% of the $10,000.00 duty paid on the imported merchandise, ignoring the mandatory 'lesser of' rule in 19 CFR § 190.32(c) when the substituted exported goods have a lower value.
distractors.E: $10,000.00 is 100% of the imported duty paid, ignoring both the 99% drawback limit and the § 190.32(c) 'lesser of' rule.

questions.stem: While reviewing shipping documents prior to filing a consumption entry for client Global Auto Parts Inc., licensed customs broker David Chen discovers an email attachment showing that the foreign seller issued two separate invoices for the same shipment: a 'Customs Invoice' for $45,000 and a secret 'Supplemental Tooling & Price Adjustment Invoice' for $30,000 that Global Auto Parts wired separately to the seller's bank account. When Chen contacts Global Auto Parts' import manager, the manager instructs Chen to file the entry declaring only the $45,000 invoice and delete the supplemental invoice email. Under 19 CFR § 111.32, what is Broker Chen legally required to do?

options.text: File the entry at $45,000 as instructed by the principal under the Power of Attorney, because the Importer of Record bears sole legal liability for valuation accuracy under 19 U.S.C. 1484.
File the entry at $45,000 to avoid General Order storage fees, and then file a Post Summary Correction (PSC) within 180 days without informing the client.

Promptly advise the client in writing of the noncompliance/omission and the required corrective action (declaring the full $75,000 transaction value), retain a copy of the written communication in his records, and refuse to file the false entry or participate in the transaction when the client refuses to correct it.
Immediately confiscate the importer's merchandise, arrest the import manager, and assess a $30,000 civil penalty on behalf of CBP.
Provide oral advice only over the telephone so that no discoverable paper trail exists, and continue filing entries for the client using the lower invoice values.

questions.goldenQuote: If a broker knows that a client has not complied with the law or has made an error in, or omission from, any document, affidavit, or other paper which the law requires the client to execute, the broker must promptly advise the client in writing of that noncompliance, error, or omission, must instruct the client on the proper corrective action required under the law, and must retain a copy of the written communication as a record under § 111.23.
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): A licensed customs broker is strictly prohibited from filing any document known to be false and has an affirmative regulatory duty when discovering client noncompliance or omission.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 111 → § 111.32 ('False information') and examine paragraphs (a), (b), and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Notice that under 19 CFR § 111.32(b) and (c), the broker's advice to the client regarding noncompliance and corrective action MUST be in writing and retained as a record under § 111.23, and the broker must refuse to file when the client refuses to correct a known false declaration.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 111.32(a), a broker must never file or assist in filing any claim or document known by the broker to be false. Under § 111.32(b), when a broker knows that a client has not complied with the law or has made an error in or omission from any required document, the broker must promptly advise the client in writing of the noncompliance, error, or omission, instruct the client on the proper corrective action, and retain a copy of that written communication for 5 years under § 111.23. Furthermore, under § 111.32(c), if the client refuses to correct the known false valuation and attempts to induce the broker to file the fraudulent $45,000 invoice, the broker must refuse to file the entry, separate from the noncompliant conduct, and document the refusal/termination.

distractors.A: Filing a document known by the broker to be false violates 19 CFR § 111.32(a) and subjects the broker to license revocation and a $30,000 monetary penalty under § 111.53 and § 111.91.
distractors.B: Knowingly filing a false entry with the intent to amend it later still violates the absolute prohibition in 19 CFR § 111.32(a) against filing a known false document.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Follows the exact mandatory steps of 19 CFR § 111.32(a), (b), and (c).
distractors.D: A customs broker is a private licensee, not a federal law enforcement officer, and has no authority to confiscate cargo, make arrests, or assess CBP penalties.
distractors.E: Oral-only advice and continued participation in double-invoicing directly violate 19 CFR § 111.32(a)–(c).

questions.stem: Three years ago, U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued a binding tariff classification ruling letter (NY N310455) to Lumina Lighting Inc. classifying its smart LED ceiling panels under an HTSUS subheading with a Free rate of duty. Following a recent Court of International Trade decision on multi-function electronics, CBP Headquarters determines that ruling NY N310455 is legally incorrect and decides to revoke it in favor of a subheading carrying a 3.9% duty rate. Under 19 CFR § 177.9(d) (and 19 U.S.C. 1625(c)), what notice-and-comment procedure and effective-date timeline must CBP follow to revoke a ruling letter that has been in effect for at least 60 days?

options.text: CBP may revoke the ruling immediately via an internal port directive, and the 3.9% duty rate applies retroactively to all unliquidated and liquidated entries filed during the past 5 years.

CBP must publish a proposed revocation notice in the Customs Bulletin with at least a 30-calendar-day public comment period, publish the final revocation decision in the Customs Bulletin within 30 calendar days after the close of the comment period, and the final revocation becomes effective 60 calendar days after the date of publication of the final notice.
CBP must send a certified letter to the ruling holder giving 10 working days' notice, after which the revocation becomes effective immediately.
Once a binding classification ruling letter has been in effect for more than 1 year, CBP is permanently barred from modifying or revoking it unless Congress amends the HTSUS statute.
CBP must publish a final revocation notice in the Federal Register that takes effect 180 calendar days after publication, with no prior public comment period required.

questions.goldenQuote: (3) Effective date — 60 calendar days after publication. The final ruling or decision modifying or revoking a prior interpretive ruling or decision will become effective 60 calendar days after the date of publication of the final notice in the Customs Bulletin.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR → Part 177 → § 177.9 (Effect of ruling letters; modification or revocation with 60-day notice)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Binding ruling letters in effect for 60 days or more cannot be revoked overnight; federal law mandates publication in a specific CBP periodical with public comment and a delayed effective date.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 177 → § 177.9 and read paragraph (d)(1), (d)(2), and (d)(3).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check the three exact timeframes in § 177.9(d): publication in the Customs Bulletin → 30 calendar days for public comment → publication of final decision within 30 calendar days after comment period closes → effective 60 calendar days after final publication.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 177.9(d)(1)–(3) and 19 U.S.C. 1625(c), when CBP seeks to modify or revoke a prior interpretive ruling or decision that has been in effect for at least 60 calendar days, CBP must: (1) publish a notice of proposed modification or revocation in the Customs Bulletin providing at least 30 calendar days for public comment; (2) publish the final ruling or decision in the Customs Bulletin within 30 calendar days after the close of the public comment period; and (3) delay the effective date of the final modification or revocation until 60 calendar days after the date of publication of the final notice in the Customs Bulletin.

distractors.A: Incorrect because immediate revocation without notice and retroactive application to entries covered by an existing ruling letter are barred by 19 CFR § 177.9(d).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Matches the exact statutory and regulatory timeline in 19 CFR § 177.9(d)(1)–(3).
distractors.C: Incorrect because a 10-working-day private letter bypasses the mandatory Customs Bulletin public notice-and-comment process and 60-day effective date delay.
distractors.D: Incorrect because CBP always retains legal authority to modify or revoke erroneous rulings prospectively by following the § 177.9(d) procedure.
distractors.E: Incorrect because proposed revocations are published in the Customs Bulletin with a mandatory 30-day public comment period and a 60-calendar-day (not 180-day) effective date delay.

questions.goldenQuote: (iv) Engineering, development, artwork, design work, and plans and sketches that are undertaken elsewhere than in the United States (i.e., OUTSIDE the United States) and are necessary for the production of the imported merchandise.
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR → Part 152 → § 152.102 (Definitions: Assist, Related persons, Identical/Similar merchandise)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Evaluate each of the 5 items against the four exclusive categories of an 'assist' in 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1) and the assist valuation rule in § 152.102(a)(3).
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 152 → § 152.102(a) and check how foreign-undertaken engineering (Milan, Italy) differs from U.S.-undertaken engineering (Minneapolis, MN).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Include Item 1 ($22,000 incorporated silicone tubing), Item 2 ($15,000 Italian engineering undertaken outside the U.S.), and Item 5 ($1,200 freight to transport the tubing assist to the factory). Exclude Item 3 (U.S.-domiciled engineering) and Item 4 (office A/C not used in production of the merchandise).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1)–(3), we evaluate each item: (1) The $22,000 biocompatible silicone tubing is an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(i) because it is a material/component incorporated in the imported merchandise; (2) The $15,000 CAD/CAM engineering blueprints developed in Milan, Italy are an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) because they constitute engineering/design work undertaken OUTSIDE the United States and necessary for production; (3) The $18,000 engineering work performed in Minneapolis by U.S.-domiciled employees is explicitly EXCLUDED from being an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) and (a)(2); (4) The $12,000 administrative office air conditioner is NOT an assist because it is not a tool/die/mold used in production of the catheters nor consumed in production; and (5) The $1,200 air courier cost to transport the silicone tubing assist to the Costa Rican factory is added to the value of the assist under § 152.102(a)(3). Total dutiable assist value = $22,000 + $15,000 + $1,200 = $38,200.

distractors.A: $22,000 includes only the silicone tubing and omits both the foreign engineering blueprints ($15,000) and the freight to transport the tubing to the foreign plant ($1,200).
distractors.B: $37,000 includes the silicone tubing ($22,000) and the Italian engineering ($15,000) but forgets to add the $1,200 transportation cost of delivering the assist to the foreign place of production under § 152.102(a)(3).
distractors.C: CORRECT ($38,200): $22,000 incorporated tubing + $15,000 foreign engineering (Italy) + $1,200 assist transport cost to the factory.
distractors.D: $56,200 erroneously includes the $18,000 U.S.-based engineering work performed in Minneapolis, which is excluded under 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) and (a)(2).
distractors.E: $68,200 erroneously includes every single item, including U.S. engineering ($18,000) and non-production office air conditioning ($12,000).

questions.stem:
Symphony Imports LLC enters a single ocean container from Japan containing two commercial product lines:
• Line 1: 200 professional acoustic guitars (Heading 9202) and 250 hard-shell molded guitar cases specially shaped and fitted to hold the guitars and suitable for long-term use (200 of the cases contain the imported guitars, while the remaining 50 identical empty cases are packed in a separate carton as spare replacement cases for Symphony's retail store).
• Line 2: 80 heavy-duty seamless high-pressure steel gas cylinders (Heading 7311) imported filled with compressed argon gas (Heading 2804); the steel cylinders are equipped with refill valves and are designed to be returned, refilled, and circulated repeatedly for 15 years.

Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 5 (GRI 5(a) and GRI 5(b)), how must the guitar cases and the steel gas cylinders be classified?

options.text: All 250 guitar cases are classified with the guitars under Heading 9202 pursuant to GRI 5(a), and all 80 steel cylinders are classified with the argon gas under Heading 2804 pursuant to GRI 5(b).

Only the 200 guitar cases entered with the 200 guitars are classified with the guitars under Heading 9202 pursuant to GRI 5(a), while the 50 excess spare guitar cases must be classified separately under Heading 4202; furthermore, the 80 heavy-duty reusable steel gas cylinders must be classified separately under Heading 7311 because GRI 5(b) is not binding on packing containers clearly suitable for repetitive use.

All 250 guitar cases must be classified separately under Heading 4202 because hard-shell cases are durable goods, while the 80 steel cylinders are classified with the argon gas under Heading 2804 pursuant to GRI 5(b).

Only the 200 guitar cases entered with the guitars are classified under Heading 9202 (with the 50 spare cases in Heading 4202), while the 80 steel cylinders are classified as argon gas under Heading 2804 because all containers entered with goods classify with their contents under GRI 5(b).
Both the guitars with cases and the cylinders with argon gas are classified under Heading 9202 and Heading 7311 respectively by application of GRI 3(c) (last in numerical order).

questions.goldenQuote: (b) Packing Materials and Packing Containers: Subject to the provisions of Rule 5(a) above, packing materials and packing containers entered with the goods therein shall be classified with the goods if they are of a kind normally used for packing such goods. However, this provision is not binding when such packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use.
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI → GRI 1–6 → HTSUS GRI 5 (Rule 5(a) Fitted Camera/Instrument Cases & Rule 5(b) Packing Containers)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): GRI 5 governs special containers and packing materials, but both Rule 5(a) and Rule 5(b) contain critical exceptions tested heavily on the CBLE.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI → GRI 1–6 → HTSUS GRI 5 and inspect the 'Crucial Exam Traps' under both Rule 5(a) and Rule 5(b).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under GRI 5(a), fitted musical instrument cases classify with the instruments ONLY to the extent they are matched 1-to-1 with the entered instruments (200 cases in 9202; 50 excess cases in 4202). Under GRI 5(b), packing containers 'clearly suitable for repetitive use' (like heavy-duty refillable steel gas cylinders) are excluded from classifying with their contents and classify separately in Heading 7311!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 5(a), musical instrument cases that are specially shaped or fitted, suitable for long-term use, and entered with the articles for which they are intended are classified with those articles (Heading 9202). However, the 50 extra guitar cases imported in excess of the 200 guitars are not 'entered with the articles for which they are intended' on a 1-to-1 basis and must be classified separately on their own merits under Heading 4202. Under HTSUS GRI 5(b), ordinary packing containers entered with goods are classified with the goods, EXCEPT that 'this provision is not binding when such packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use.' Heavy-duty seamless steel compressed-gas cylinders designed for 15 years of continuous refilling and return circulation are the classic example of repetitive-use containers and must be classified separately under Heading 7311 rather than with the argon gas (Heading 2804).

distractors.A: Erroneously classifies the 50 excess spare guitar cases under GRI 5(a) and ignores the repetitive-use exception in GRI 5(b) for the refillable steel cylinders.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Applies both the 1-to-1 matching requirement of GRI 5(a) (200 cases in 9202; 50 excess cases in 4202) and the repetitive-use exception of GRI 5(b) (80 refillable steel cylinders in 7311).
distractors.C: Erroneously rejects GRI 5(a) for the 200 fitted cases entered with the guitars and ignores the GRI 5(b) repetitive-use exception for the steel cylinders.
distractors.D: Correctly splits the 200 vs. 50 guitar cases under GRI 5(a), but fails to apply the GRI 5(b) exception for packing containers clearly suitable for repetitive use.
distractors.E: GRI 3(c) does not apply to containers and packing materials governed specifically by GRI 5(a) and GRI 5(b).

questions.stem:
Atlantic Trade Brokerage Inc., a licensed corporate customs broker headquartered in Newark, NJ, relocates its customs entry record archive to a new facility and designates a new Recordkeeping Point of Contact on October 1. In addition, Atlantic Trade Brokerage is auditing its retention schedule for three categories of documents:
(1) Standard consumption entry files (CBP Form 7501, commercial invoices, packing lists);
(2) A corporate Power of Attorney (POA) that was revoked by an active client on June 15, 2024; and
(3) Records supporting a Modernized Drawback claim that was liquidated and paid on August 10, 2025.

Under 19 CFR § 111.23 (and § 190.51(f)), where must the broker's original records be maintained, within how many days must the broker notify CBP of the change in record storage location/point of contact, and what are the mandatory retention periods for these three categories of records?

options.text: Records may be stored anywhere in North America (U.S., Canada, or Mexico); notify CBP within 60 calendar days; retain entry files for 3 years from entry, revoked POAs for 2 years from revocation, and drawback records for 5 years from entry.

Records must be maintained within the customs territory of the United States; notify the Broker Management Branch within 30 calendar days of the change; retain standard entry files for 5 years from the date of entry, revoked POAs for 5 years after the date of revocation (or 5 years after the client ceases to be an active client, whichever is later), and drawback claim records for 3 years after liquidation of the drawback claim.

Records must be maintained within the customs territory of the United States; notify CBP within 10 working days of the change; retain all entry files, revoked POAs, and drawback records for 7 years from the end of the calendar year.

Records must be maintained at the port of entry where each shipment arrived; notify CBP on the Triennial Status Report only; retain entry files for 5 years from liquidation and revoked POAs permanently.

Records may be stored on foreign cloud servers outside the U.S. customs territory without domestic access; notify CBP within 30 working days; retain entry files and drawback records for 3 years from date of importation.

questions.goldenQuote: (c) Notification of change of record storage location or point of contact. Within 30 calendar days of any change to the place of retention of records or the designated recordkeeping point of contact (including name, telephone number, or email address), the broker must electronically notify the Broker Management Branch (or submit written notification if electronic transmission is unavailable) of the new location or updated contact information.
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the three pillars of broker recordkeeping: geographic location requirement, notification deadline for changing storage location/contact, and specific retention timelines.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 111 → § 111.23(a), (b), and (c), and cross-reference § 190.51(f) for drawback record retention.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Original records must be kept within the U.S. customs territory; notification to the Broker Management Branch is due within 30 calendar days; entry records = 5 years from date of entry; revoked POA = 5 years from revocation or last active client date (whichever is later); drawback records = 3 years from liquidation of the drawback claim.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 111.23(a), a licensed customs broker must maintain originals of all required customs records within the customs territory of the United States. Under § 111.23(c), within 30 calendar days of any change to the place of retention of records or the designated recordkeeping point of contact, the broker must notify the Broker Management Branch. Under § 111.23(b), standard entry records must be retained for at least 5 years after the date of entry, while revoked powers of attorney must be retained for 5 years after the date of revocation or 5 years after the date the client ceases to be an 'active client' (whichever period is later). Finally, under 19 CFR § 190.51(f) (and § 163.4(b)(1)), records supporting a drawback claim must be retained for at least 3 years after liquidation of the drawback claim.

distractors.A: Incorrect on all counts: records cannot be stored outside the U.S. customs territory, notification is 30 calendar days (not 60), and entry/POA retention is 5 years.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately states the U.S. customs territory requirement, the 30-calendar-day notification window, the 5-year entry and revoked POA rules under § 111.23, and the 3-year post-liquidation drawback retention rule under § 190.51(f).
distractors.C: Incorrect because notification is 30 calendar days (not 10 working days) and CBP does not use a 7-year tax-style retention period.
distractors.D: Incorrect because national permit holders maintain records centrally within the U.S. customs territory (not at every arrival port), must notify CBP within 30 calendar days (not wait for the Triennial Status Report), and count the 5-year entry retention period from the date of entry (not liquidation).
distractors.E: Incorrect because records must be maintained within the U.S. customs territory and entry retention is 5 years from the date of entry.

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Expansion Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Sarah Jenkins is retained by a new business client, Oakridge Landscaping LLC, to prepare its current-year federal income tax return. While reviewing the prior year's tax return (which was prepared by a different accountant) alongside Oakridge's general ledger, Jenkins discovers that the client omitted $140,000 of taxable cash landscaping receipts from the prior year's Schedule C. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.21), what are Jenkins' exact legal obligations upon discovering the client's prior-year omission?

options.text: Promptly notify the IRS Criminal Investigation Division in writing of the $140,000 omission and transmit copies of the client's general ledger to the IRS.
Prepare and electronically file an amended Form 1040-X for the prior year on the client's behalf immediately, even if the client refuses to sign or authorize the amended return.

Promptly advise the client of the fact of the noncompliance, error, or omission, AND advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission (without unilaterally notifying the IRS).
Ignore the prior-year omission completely because Jenkins did not sign or prepare the prior year's tax return.
Automatically report the prior tax preparer to the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) within 15 calendar days and impound the client's accounting records.

questions.goldenQuote: A practitioner who, having been retained by a client with respect to a matter administered by the Internal Revenue Service, knows that the client has not complied with the revenue laws of the United States or has made an error in or omission from any return, document, affidavit, or other paper which the client submitted or executed under the revenue laws of the United States, must advise the client promptly of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission. The practitioner must advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission.

socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Compare how IRS Circular 230 handles a client's tax omission with how 19 CFR § 111.32 handles a customs client's error.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Switch to the '31 CFR Part 10' corpus tab → Subpart B → § 10.21 ('Knowledge of client's omission').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under 31 CFR § 10.21, the practitioner must promptly advise the client of (1) the fact of the error/omission AND (2) the consequences under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations. The practitioner is NEVER allowed to report the client's omission to the IRS unilaterally or file an amended return without client consent!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.21 (Circular 230), a practitioner who knows that a client has not complied with the U.S. revenue laws or has made an error in or omission from any return or document submitted under the revenue laws (regardless of who prepared the prior return) has two mandatory duties: (1) promptly advise the client of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission; and (2) advise the client of the consequences under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations (such as accuracy-related penalties, interest, and statute of limitations implications). Circular 230 does NOT authorize the practitioner to inform the IRS without client consent, nor can a practitioner file an amended return without the taxpayer's authorization.

distractors.A: Unilaterally disclosing confidential client tax information to the IRS without a lawful summons or client consent violates IRC § 7216 and is not permitted by Circular 230 § 10.21.
distractors.B: A practitioner cannot file an amended tax return (Form 1040-X) without the client's signature and authorization.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Accurately states the two mandatory practitioner obligations under 31 CFR § 10.21.
distractors.D: 31 CFR § 10.21 applies whenever a retained practitioner discovers a client's error or omission on any submitted return, even if another preparer signed the prior-year return.
distractors.E: Circular 230 § 10.21 does not mandate reporting the prior preparer within 15 days or impounding client records (in fact, § 10.28 requires returning client records promptly upon request).

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Expansion Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Marcus Vance is preparing an individual federal income tax return for a client who wants to claim an aggressive business deduction that is NOT a tax shelter or reportable transaction. After researching the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury regulations, and Tax Court precedent, Vance concludes that the deduction has approximately a 25% likelihood of being sustained on its merits—meaning it satisfies the 'Reasonable Basis' standard (~20% or higher) but falls short of 'Substantial Authority' (~40% or higher). In addition, the client hands Vance a handwritten summary of travel expenses that directly contradicts the client's bank statements. Under 31 CFR § 10.34(a), (c), and (d), under what conditions may Vance sign the return containing the deduction, and how must Vance handle the contradictory travel expense summary?

options.text: Vance may sign the return without disclosing the deduction because any non-frivolous position (>5% likelihood) is permissible without disclosure, and Vance may accept the client's handwritten travel summary without inquiry because preparers never verify client data.

Vance may sign the return containing the deduction ONLY if the position is adequately disclosed to the IRS (e.g., on Form 8275) because it has a Reasonable Basis (~25%) rather than Substantial Authority (~40%), must inform the client of potential penalties and the opportunity to avoid them through disclosure, and MUST make reasonable inquiries regarding the travel expenses because a practitioner may not ignore client-furnished information that appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.
Vance is strictly prohibited from signing the return even with Form 8275 disclosure because every position on a tax return must meet the 'More Likely Than Not' (>50%) standard.

Vance may sign the return without disclosure if the client signs a hold-harmless waiver, but Vance must independently audit every single canceled check and receipt for all categories on the tax return.
Vance must require a 75% certainty level before signing any tax return and must report the contradictory travel summary to the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility.

questions.goldenQuote: The practitioner may not, however, ignore the implications of information furnished to, or actually known by, the practitioner, and must make reasonable inquiries if the information as furnished appears to be incorrect, inconsistent with an important fact or another factual assumption, or incomplete.
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 → Subpart B → § 10.34 (Standards with respect to tax returns and documents)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Distinguish the confidence threshold required for an UNDISCLOSED tax position ('Substantial Authority') versus an ADEQUATELY DISCLOSED non-tax-shelter position ('Reasonable Basis'), and check the rule on client-furnished information.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 → Subpart B → § 10.34 and read paragraphs (a)(1)-(2), (c), and (d).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): A non-tax-shelter position with a Reasonable Basis (~25%) can be signed ONLY if adequately disclosed (Form 8275). And under § 10.34(d), while a practitioner generally relies in good faith on client information without audit, the practitioner MUST make reasonable inquiries when the information appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.34(a) (incorporating IRC § 6694(a)(2)), a practitioner may not sign a tax return containing a non-tax-shelter position unless it either (1) has 'Substantial Authority' (~40% or greater likelihood of being sustained) if undisclosed, OR (2) has at least a 'Reasonable Basis' (~20% or greater likelihood) AND is adequately disclosed to the IRS on Form 8275 (or Form 8275-R). Since the position has a ~25% likelihood, it satisfies Reasonable Basis and may be signed only if adequately disclosed. Under § 10.34(c), Vance must also inform the client of potential penalties and the opportunity to avoid them through disclosure. Finally, under § 10.34(d), although a practitioner may generally rely in good faith without verification on client-furnished information, the practitioner may NOT ignore the implications of information known to the practitioner and MUST make reasonable inquiries when the furnished information appears incorrect, inconsistent with other facts, or incomplete.

distractors.A: Incorrect because an undisclosed position requires Substantial Authority (~40%), a mere 'non-frivolous' standard was replaced by 'Reasonable Basis' for disclosed positions, and § 10.34(d) prohibits ignoring contradictory client data.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately applies the Reasonable Basis + Adequate Disclosure (Form 8275) standard under § 10.34(a), the penalty disclosure rule under § 10.34(c), and the duty of reasonable inquiry for inconsistent client data under § 10.34(d).
distractors.C: Incorrect because the 'More Likely Than Not' (>50%) standard applies only to tax shelters and reportable transactions, not ordinary business deductions.
distractors.D: Incorrect because a client waiver cannot override Circular 230 § 10.34 standards, and § 10.34(d) does not require auditing unimpeached client figures that appear consistent and complete.
distractors.E: Incorrect because neither a 75% certainty threshold nor reporting a client to OPR exists under Circular 230 § 10.34.
